outages.cause: Rolling and emergency blackouts after Russian attacks on energy infrastructure, including a large-scale attack on Nov 20, further strikes reported on subsequent days, including overnight and on the morning of Wednesday, Nov 25, additional Wednesday afternoon strikes in several regions, and further strikes that Ukrenergo said took place during Thursday, Nov 26. Ukrenergo, as reported by LB.ua at 9:53 a.m. Saturday, Nov 28, said that as of that hour emergency power cuts were in effect in Kyiv region after the impact of Russian shelling and equipment overloads, and that a return to scheduled hourly outages would be possible as soon as the situation in the power system allowed. DTEK, as reported by Ukrinform at 10:40 a.m. Saturday, Nov 28, said that on Ukrenergo's command emergency outages were in effect in Buchanskyi, Obukhivskyi, and Fastivskyi districts of Kyiv region, and that the schedules were not working. Ukrenergo, as reported by UNIAN at 9:37 p.m. Friday, Nov 27, had said that on Saturday, Nov 28, consumption restrictions would be applied in some regions of Ukraine: hourly outage schedules of 1 to 3 queues for all categories of consumers, and capacity-limitation schedules for industry. The same UNIAN report, citing Ukrenergo, said a difficult electricity-supply situation remained in Zaporizhzhia and Dnipropetrovsk regions, where emergency outages continued to be applied because of damage to energy infrastructure from Russian shelling, and that energy workers had managed to normalize the electricity-supply situation in Kherson region. The Energy Ministry, as reported in Wednesday morning accounts, and the IAEA, as reported by TASS citing an IAEA press-service statement, had said the temporarily occupied Zaporizhzhia Nuclear Power Plant had lost its external power supply and switched to diesel generators. The IAEA, in Update 377 dated Nov 26, 2026, said the plant's connection to its sole remaining external power line, the 330 kV Ferosplavna-1 line, was lost on Nov 25 at 5:28 a.m. local time, reportedly due to military activity, that this was the 28th time during the conflict that ZNPP was relying on emergency diesel generators, and that the IAEA was engaging with the Russian Federation and Ukraine on arrangements for a ninth localized ceasefire to facilitate repair of the line. ZNPP communications director Yevgenia Yashina, as reported by TASS on Nov 26 from Melitopol, said that as of the morning of Nov 26 the Ferrosplavnaya-1 line remained disconnected, that the location of the malfunction had been identified, and that it was still too early to say when electricity would be restored.
outages.affected: Ukrenergo, as reported by LB.ua at 9:53 a.m. Saturday, Nov 28 (2:53 a.m. CT), said that as of that hour emergency power cuts were in effect in Kyiv region after the impact of Russian shelling and equipment overloads, that a return to scheduled hourly outages would be possible as soon as the situation in the power system allowed, and that repair crews had already begun restoration work. The same report, citing Ukrenergo, said the electricity-supply situation remained difficult in Zaporizhzhia and Dnipropetrovsk regions, where emergency power cuts continued because of significant damage to energy infrastructure. DTEK, as reported by Ukrinform at 10:40 a.m. Saturday, Nov 28 (3:40 a.m. CT), said that on Ukrenergo's command emergency outages were in effect in Buchanskyi, Obukhivskyi, and Fastivskyi districts of Kyiv region, and that the schedules were not working. Glavcom, in a report published at 10:21 a.m. Saturday, Nov 28 (3:21 a.m. CT), citing Ukrenergo and DTEK, likewise said emergency outages were in effect in those three districts of Kyiv region, that the usual hourly schedules were not working there, and that the restrictions were caused by the consequences of Russian shelling and equipment overloads. UNN, in a report published at 7:46 a.m. Saturday, Nov 28 (12:46 a.m. CT), quoting Ukrenergo, said that because of the consequences of enemy shelling and equipment overloads, emergency outages were in effect in Kyiv region as of that hour, and that a return to hourly outage schedules would take place as soon as the situation in the power system allowed. Ukrenergo, as reported by UNIAN at 9:37 p.m. Friday, Nov 27 (1:37 p.m. CT), had said that on Saturday, Nov 28, consumption restrictions would be applied in some regions of Ukraine: hourly outage schedules of 1 to 3 queues for all categories of consumers, which UNIAN said means from 4 to 12 hours without electricity, and capacity-limitation schedules for industry. The same UNIAN report also published Saturday operator schedules, including Kharkiv region hourly schedules from 12:00 a.m. to 12:00 a.m. Saturday under which outages would last a minimum of 4 hours 30 minutes and a maximum of 15 hours; Poltava region schedules under which outages would last from 7 to 10 hours a day; Cherkasy region schedules from 6:00 a.m. to 12:00 a.m. Saturday under which outages would last from 6 to 8 hours a day depending on the sub-queue; Rivne region schedules under which each sub-queue would be without electricity for 2 hours a day; and Khmelnytskyi region schedules under which total outage duration would be from 5 to 10 hours a day depending on the sub-queue. The IAEA, in Update 377 dated Nov 26, 2026, said the Zaporizhzhia Nuclear Power Plant's connection to its sole remaining external power line, the 330 kV Ferosplavna-1 line, was lost on Nov 25 at 5:28 a.m. local time, reportedly due to military activity, that this was the 28th time during the conflict that ZNPP was relying on emergency diesel generators, that the IAEA was engaging with both sides on arrangements for a ninth localized ceasefire to facilitate repair of the line, and that the IAEA estimated the plant had sufficient diesel fuel to maintain its then-current configuration of two operating emergency diesel generators for more than ten days. TASS, in a Nov 26 report from Melitopol, quoted ZNPP communications director Yevgenia Yashina as saying that as of the morning of Nov 26, the Ferrosplavnaya-1 line remained disconnected, that the location of the malfunction had been identified, and that it was still too early to say when electricity would be restored. No official nationwide customer count was found as of 6:00 AM CT Saturday, Nov 28 (1:00 p.m. Saturday, Nov 28, EET), and no later official confirmation that ZNPP external power had been restored was found.

outages.place: Odesa, including Peresypskyi district and Odesa district, and other parts of Odesa and Odesa region
outages.cause: Repeated Russian attacks on high-voltage transmission networks and other energy facilities critical to the region, including a strike on a DTEK Odeski Elektromerezhi energy facility on the morning of Nov 20, further damage reported over Nov 24-25, a massive strike-drone attack on Odesa and its suburbs on the afternoon of Wednesday, Nov 25, and a further attack on energy infrastructure in Odesa region on Saturday, Nov 28. Novyny.LIVE, in a report published at 12:46 p.m. Saturday, Nov 28, citing DTEK Odeski Elektromerezhi, said Russian forces had again attacked energy infrastructure in Odesa region on Saturday, that a DTEK facility was damaged, and that because of a network accident Peresypskyi district of Odesa and Odesa district of the region were partially de-energized, with stabilization outage schedules not in effect in those areas. Odessa Life, in a report published at 10:22 a.m. Saturday, Nov 28, said the Saturday stabilization-outage schedule for Odesa and Odesa region had been updated at 10:19 a.m. Saturday and would continue to apply to all 12 of the company's schedule groups, with hours subject to change on Ukrenergo's commands.
outages.affected: Novyny.LIVE, in a report published at 12:46 p.m. Saturday, Nov 28 (5:46 a.m. CT), citing DTEK Odeski Elektromerezhi, said that on Saturday, Nov 28, Russian forces had again attacked energy infrastructure in Odesa region, that because of damage to a DTEK facility more than 6,000 families had been left without electricity, and that energy workers had begun inspecting surviving equipment and clearing debris when the security situation allowed, with restoration expected to take time. The same report, citing DTEK, said that because of a network accident, Peresypskyi district of Odesa and Odesa district of the region were partially de-energized, and that stabilization outage schedules were not in effect in those areas. The same report said that on Saturday, on Ukrenergo's command, stabilization outages were in effect in part of Odesa and the region for all six consumer groups, with total outage duration from 4 to 11.5 hours, and published this updated group timetable: group 1.1, 6:00 a.m. to 9:00 a.m. and 3:30 p.m. to 8:30 p.m.; group 1.2, 10:00 a.m. to 12:30 p.m. and 4:00 p.m. to 10:30 p.m.; group 2.1, 10:30 a.m. to 12:30 p.m. and 3:30 p.m. to 7:30 p.m.; group 2.2, 6:00 a.m. to 9:00 a.m., 10:30 a.m. to 12:30 p.m., and 3:30 p.m. to 7:30 p.m.; group 3.1, 8:30 a.m. to 4:00 p.m. and 7:00 p.m. to 11:00 p.m.; group 3.2, 8:30 a.m. to 2:30 p.m. and 7:00 p.m. to 10:30 p.m.; groups 4.1 and 4.2, 7:00 p.m. to 11:00 p.m.; group 5.1, 12:00 p.m. to 4:00 p.m. and 7:00 p.m. to 7:30 p.m.; group 5.2, 12:00 p.m. to 7:30 p.m. and 10:30 p.m. to 12:00 a.m.; group 6.1, 6:00 a.m. to 7:30 a.m., 2:00 p.m. to 7:00 p.m., and 10:30 p.m. to 12:00 a.m.; and group 6.2, 12:00 p.m. to 4:00 p.m. and 10:30 p.m. to 12:00 a.m. Odessa Life, in a report published at 10:22 a.m. Saturday, Nov 28 (3:22 a.m. CT), said the Saturday schedule had been updated at 10:19 a.m. Saturday and published an earlier Saturday table for all 12 groups; that earlier table was followed later in the morning by the Novyny.LIVE 12:46 p.m. update citing DTEK. No later official customer count for Odesa or Odesa region, beyond the more than 6,000 families cited in the Saturday Novyny.LIVE report of the new attack, was found as of 6:00 AM CT Saturday, Nov 28 (1:00 p.m. Saturday, Nov 28, EET).

outages.place: Dnipro and parts of Dnipropetrovsk region, including Dniprovskyi, Samarivskyi, Synelnykivskyi, and Pavlohradskyi districts
outages.cause: Russian attacks on energy facilities in Dnipropetrovsk region, including strikes on Nov 24 and overnight into Nov 25, a Wednesday, Nov 25, attack on one of DTEK's thermal power plants, a later Wednesday attack that DTEK said damaged main power grids, and further strikes that Ukrenergo said took place during Thursday, Nov 26. DTEK, as reported by Glavcom at 10:21 a.m. Saturday, Nov 28, and by UNN at 7:46 a.m. Saturday, said Russian attacks had caused significant damage to the region's energy infrastructure, making the usual queue and sub-queue schedules impossible to apply, and that individual outage schedules were being calculated separately for each building. Ukrenergo, as reported by LB.ua at 9:53 a.m. Saturday, Nov 28, said the electricity-supply situation remained difficult in Dnipropetrovsk and Zaporizhzhia regions and that emergency power cuts continued in those regions because of significant damage to energy infrastructure. Ukrenergo, as reported by UNIAN at 9:37 p.m. Friday, Nov 27, had likewise said emergency outages continued to be applied in Dnipropetrovsk region because of damage to energy infrastructure from Russian shelling.
outages.affected: DTEK, as reported by Glavcom at 10:21 a.m. Saturday, Nov 28 (3:21 a.m. CT), and by UNN at 7:46 a.m. Saturday (12:46 a.m. CT), said individual outage schedules had been introduced in Dnipropetrovsk region because Russian attacks had caused significant damage to the region's energy infrastructure, making the usual queue and sub-queue schedules impossible to apply. The same accounts, citing DTEK Dniprovski Elektromerezhi, said energy workers were calculating outage hours separately for each building, that even neighboring buildings could be cut at different times because they may be fed from different lines, that the next day's schedules are published each evening, and that hours could change during the day if Ukrenergo updated its restriction commands. Ukrenergo, as reported by LB.ua at 9:53 a.m. Saturday, Nov 28 (2:53 a.m. CT), said the electricity-supply situation remained difficult in Zaporizhzhia and Dnipropetrovsk regions and that emergency power cuts continued in those regions because of significant damage to energy infrastructure. Ukrenergo, as reported by UNIAN at 9:37 p.m. Friday, Nov 27 (1:37 p.m. CT), had said a difficult electricity-supply situation remained in those two regions and that emergency outages continued to be applied in both because of damage to energy infrastructure from Russian shelling. Dniprovska poradnytsia, in a report published at 10:22 a.m. Friday, Nov 27 (2:22 a.m. CT), citing DTEK, had said emergency outages were in effect in Dnipro and in the Dniprovskyi, Pavlohradskyi, Synelnykivskyi, and Samarivskyi districts, and that schedules were also not in effect for Central Energy Company (TSEK) customers in Dnipro and Pavlohrad. No official customer count for Dnipro or Dnipropetrovsk region was found as of 6:00 AM CT Saturday, Nov 28 (1:00 p.m. Saturday, Nov 28, EET).

outages.place: Kurdistan Region, including Erbil, Sulaymaniyah, Duhok, Bazian, and Chamchamal
outages.cause: Suspected drone attack on the Khor Mor gas field on the night of Nov 8, 2026, which halted gas production that supplies much of the region's electricity generation. Dana Gas, the field's operator, later said the facility had sustained significant damage and could produce no gas
outages.affected: 964media, in an English-language report dated Nov 28, 2026, at 11:04 (2:04 a.m. CT Saturday, if Iraq time), citing an unnamed technical source familiar with the restart who asked not to be named because the source was not authorized to speak publicly, said the Khor Mor gas field was expected to resume production on Sunday at a third of its capacity before the Nov 8 attack. The source told 964media that production would restart at the KM250 processing unit, which can handle up to 250 million cubic feet of gas a day, that the attacked KM400 section, which had a daily production capacity of 500 million cubic feet, had had no repair work carried out on it so far, and that repairs to KM400 would take at least four to five months from the start of work. The same source said that if all of the KM250 gas were allocated to the Kurdistan Region, grid power there could rise to about 12 hours a day, and that a government decision would set how the gas is shared after the restart. The same report said production had been halted since a suspected drone attack damaged a gas processing unit, cutting grid supply across the Region from 24 hours a day to six to eight, that the Nov 8 attack knocked nearly 3,000 megawatts of generation off the Kurdistan Region's grid, and that Dana Gas, which operates the field with Crescent Petroleum, had on Nov 14 said the field had been heavily damaged and could not produce any gas, had given no timeline for resuming production, and had not publicly announced a restart. A 964media Arabic report dated 11:18 p.m. Friday, Nov 27, 2026 (2:18 p.m. CT if Iraq time), citing an unnamed technical source familiar with restart work, had already reported the same expected Sunday, Nov 29, restart at the KM250 section only, at about one-third of previous capacity, the four-to-five-month KM400 repair estimate, and the possible rise to about 12 hours a day if the entire 250 million cubic feet were allocated to the region. The KRG's Runaki electricity program, launched in October 2024 to provide round-the-clock grid power, was supplying nearly 5.5 million people, more than 85 percent of the Region's population, by April, according to the KRG Electricity Ministry, as reported in the Saturday-dated 964media account. No official confirmation that production had already resumed, and no official nationwide or Kurdistan-wide customer count or official firm restoration timetable, was found as of 6:00 AM CT Saturday, Nov 28 (3:00 p.m. Saturday, Nov 28, Iraq time).
outages.etr: No official firm restoration time was given. 964media, in an English-language report dated Nov 28, 2026, at 11:04, citing an unnamed technical source familiar with the restart, said the field was expected to resume production on Sunday at a third of its pre-attack capacity, at the KM250 unit only, and that repairing the attacked KM400 section would take at least four to five months from the start of work; the same source said electricity supply in the Kurdistan Region could rise to about 12 hours a day if the entire 250 million cubic feet were allocated to the region, which the source said was not yet decided. That was an unnamed source's expectation, not an official Dana Gas or electricity-ministry timetable, and the report did not say production had already resumed and said Dana Gas had not publicly announced a restart. No official confirmation that production had already resumed, and no official nationwide or Kurdistan-wide customer count or official firm restoration timetable, was found as of 6:00 AM CT Saturday, Nov 28 (3:00 p.m. Saturday, Nov 28, Iraq time).
outages.updated: Nov 28, 2026, 964media English-language report dated Nov 28 at 11:04 (= 2:04 a.m. CT Saturday, if Iraq time), citing an unnamed technical source, on an expected Sunday restart of the KM250 unit at about one-third of pre-attack capacity, on a four-to-five-month repair estimate for the attacked KM400 section, on a possible rise to about 12 hours of electricity a day in the Kurdistan Region if that gas were allocated entirely to the region, and on Dana Gas not having publicly announced a restart; earlier 964media Arabic report dated 11:18 p.m. Friday, Nov 27 (= 2:18 p.m. CT if Iraq time), on the same expected Sunday, Nov 29, KM250 restart; rechecked 6:00 AM CT Saturday, Nov 28 (3:00 p.m. Saturday, Nov 28, Iraq time), no official confirmation that Khor Mor gas production had already resumed was found, and no official nationwide or Kurdistan-wide customer count or official firm restoration timetable was found

outages.place: Donetsk, Makiivka, Mariupol, Yenakiieve, Snizhne, Torez, Horlivka, and nearby districts, including Kirovskyi, Kuybyshevskyi, Leninskyi, Yasynuvata, Volodarske, Amvrosiivka, and Ilovaisk
outages.cause: Attacks on energy infrastructure, including a massive attack on the night of Nov 22, 2026, according to occupation officials, who said attacks on energy facilities were repeated the following night and that new outages were added to the effects of earlier damage. Occupation officials also described a power deficit and forced temporary outages to prevent accidents. On Thursday morning, Nov 26, the occupation Ministry of Coal and Energy, as reported by DNR News, said a large volume of emergency restoration work had been carried out over the previous day and that by morning almost the entire territory was supplied with electricity, while some local outages and forced temporary outages because of a shortage of available capacity continued. Later Thursday morning, occupation Donetsk administration head Alexei Kulemzin, citing Donetskenergo, said 507 transformer substations had been partially de-energized in all districts of Donetsk because the permissible load on the network had been exceeded. On Thursday evening, Kulemzin, again citing Donetskenergo as of 7:00 p.m. Thursday, said 556 transformer substations were partially de-energized in all districts of Donetsk for the same stated reason. Later Thursday evening, Kulemzin, again citing Donetskenergo, as published by Lenta novostei Donetska at 10:30 p.m. Thursday, Nov 26, said 518 transformer substations were partially de-energized in all districts of Donetsk because the permissible load on the network had been exceeded. On Friday evening, Nov 27, Kulemzin, again citing Donetskenergo, as published by Lenta novostei DNR at 7:11 p.m. Friday, said 324 transformer substations were partially de-energized in the Budennovsky, Kalininsky, Kievsky, Kirovsky, Petrovsky, Proletarsky, and Leninsky districts because the permissible load on the network had been exceeded. On Saturday morning, Nov 28, Kulemzin, citing Donetskenergo, as reported by Ridus at 8:40 a.m. Saturday, Nov 28, said more than 23,000 subscribers in Donetsk had lost electricity supply because of the disconnection of 125 transformer substations in the Kirovsky, Kuybyshevsky, and Leninsky districts, and that because of a shortage of capacity, temporary outages were possible during the day in some municipalities of the republic to prevent accidents and protect equipment from overload.
outages.affected: Occupation Donetsk administration head Alexei Kulemzin, as reported by Ridus at 8:40 a.m. Saturday, Nov 28 (11:40 p.m. CT Friday, Nov 27, if Moscow time), citing Donetskenergo, said that more than 23,000 subscribers in Donetsk had lost electricity supply because of the disconnection of 125 transformer substations in the Kirovsky, Kuybyshevsky, and Leninsky districts, that specialists were promptly carrying out restoration work, and that because of a shortage of capacity, temporary outages were possible during the day in some municipalities of the republic to prevent accidents and protect equipment from overload. That Saturday morning figure was lower than Friday evening's figure from the same official. Occupation Donetsk administration head Alexei Kulemzin, as published by Lenta novostei DNR at 7:11 p.m. Friday, Nov 27 (10:11 a.m. CT if Moscow time), citing Donetskenergo, a branch of JSC Yugo-Zapadnaya ESK, said that because the permissible load on the network had been exceeded, 324 transformer substations were partially de-energized in the Budennovsky, Kalininsky, Kievsky, Kirovsky, Petrovsky, Proletarsky, and Leninsky districts, and that 45,315 subscribers remained without electricity, with work under way to restore electricity supply. That Friday evening figure was higher than Friday morning's figures from the same official. Kulemzin, as published by Lenta novostei Donetska at 10:02 a.m. Friday, Nov 27 (1:02 a.m. CT if Moscow time), citing Donetskenergo, had said that 295 transformer substations were partially de-energized in the Kalininsky, Kievsky, and Proletarsky districts, and that 40,500 subscribers remained without electricity, with work under way to restore electricity supply. Kulemzin, as published by Lenta novostei Donetska at 10:30 p.m. Thursday, Nov 26 (1:30 p.m. CT if Moscow time), citing Donetskenergo, had said that 518 transformer substations were partially de-energized in all districts of Donetsk, and that 44,230 subscribers remained without electricity. Earlier Thursday, Kulemzin, as reported by Ostro at 6:45 p.m. Thursday, Nov 26, and by DNR News at 7:08 p.m. Thursday, citing Donetskenergo as of 7:00 p.m. Thursday (10:00 a.m. CT if Moscow time), had said 556 transformer substations were partially de-energized in all districts of Donetsk and that 57,848 subscribers remained without electricity. KP.ru, in a report dated 7:00 a.m. Friday, Nov 27, citing the occupation Ministry of Coal and Energy, said a tense situation remained in the region's energy system, that emergency restoration work was under way in Mariupol and the Novoazovsk municipal district, with energy workers hoping to finish repairs to damaged power lines by midday, that local outages were still being recorded in some districts of Donetsk, Makiivka, Horlivka, Dokuchaievsk, Yenakiieve, Snizhne, and Kirovske, and in the Yasynuvata, Amvrosiivka, and Shakhtarsk districts, and that as of Friday morning forced temporary outages because of a shortage of available capacity were in effect in the Donetsk urban district, the Amvrosiivka and Shakhtarsk districts, and Snizhne, and could spread to other municipalities during the day, with the time and duration of those outages impossible to name in advance. Earlier Thursday morning accounts from the occupation Ministry of Coal and Energy and Kulemzin, as previously recorded, had described a still-difficult situation in the region's energy system and remaining local and forced outages.
outages.start: Night of Sunday, Nov 22, 2026, local time, for the attack described by occupation officials; occupation officials said attacks on energy facilities were repeated the following night; a further failure at about 11:00 p.m. Monday, Nov 23, was reported on Tuesday morning; other partial outages in the region were already being reported
outages.etr: No official firm restoration time was given for the remaining outages. Occupation Donetsk administration head Alexei Kulemzin, as reported by Ridus at 8:40 a.m. Saturday, Nov 28, citing Donetskenergo, said specialists were promptly carrying out restoration work and did not give a restoration time; the same account said temporary outages were possible during the day in some municipalities because of a shortage of capacity, without naming the time or duration of those possible outages in advance. No official firm restoration time was given for the remaining outages. Occupation Donetsk administration head Alexei Kulemzin, as published by Lenta novostei DNR at 7:11 p.m. Friday, Nov 27, citing Donetskenergo, said work to restore electricity supply was under way and did not give a restoration time. Earlier, Kulemzin, as published by Lenta novostei Donetska at 10:02 a.m. Friday, Nov 27, and at 7:06 p.m. Thursday, Nov 26, citing Donetskenergo, likewise said work to restore electricity supply was under way and did not give a restoration time. KP.ru, in a report dated 7:00 a.m. Friday, Nov 27, citing the occupation Ministry of Coal and Energy, said energy workers hoped to finish repairs to damaged power lines in Mariupol and the Novoazovsk municipal district by midday Friday; that was a hope for those repairs, not a firm restoration time for the remaining outages. DNR News, citing the occupation Ministry of Coal and Energy at 9:14 a.m. Thursday, Nov 26, said forced temporary outages continued in some districts because of a shortage of available capacity, and that the time and duration of those outages could not be determined in advance because decisions were made operationally based on the current load. outages.place: Crimea, including Sevastopol, Yalta, Feodosia, Yevpatoria, Saky, Armyansk, Dzhankoy, and Bilohirsk, and Nyzhnohirskyi, Saky, Sovietskyi, Chornomorskyi, Krasnoperekopsk, Bakhchysarai, Kirovskyi, Rozdolne, Pervomaiskyi, Krasnohvardiiske, and Simferopol districts
outages.cause: A further power outage in Crimea and Sevastopol on the afternoon of Thursday, Nov 26, 2026, which Krymenergo and Sevastopolenergo, as reported by RIA Novosti, attributed to an accident at energy facilities outside the peninsula. That afternoon outage came during an already announced restriction regime that occupation sources had attributed to a power-capacity shortage after strikes on transmission networks outside the peninsula, and to emergency repair work cited by occupation authorities as the reason for temporary supply restrictions beginning Wednesday, Nov 25. Krymskaya Gazeta, in a report dated 9:02 a.m. Thursday, Nov 26, citing Krymenergo, had said restrictions on the electric-power consumption regime had been introduced in the Republic of Crimea on Thursday, Nov 26, on the command of the federal System Operator, with an approximate outage duration of 3 to 12 hours. Sergei Aksenov, the occupation head of Crimea, had said Tuesday that beginning Wednesday, for a period of no more than 10 days, electricity supply would be restricted, with a planned 30 percent reduction in capacity from 8:00 a.m. to 9:00 p.m. and the peak of outages from 12:00 p.m. to 3:00 p.m., and that there would be no restrictions from 9:00 p.m. to 8:00 a.m.; RIA Novosti said those hours were Moscow time. On Saturday morning, Nov 28, 2026, after Sevastopolenergo had said electricity supply to all consumers in Sevastopol was restored at 1:00 a.m. Saturday until the next command to introduce restrictions, Sevastopolenergo, as reported by Sev-news at 6:36 a.m. Saturday, Nov 28, said that on the command of the ChRDU dispatcher a temporary electricity-supply restriction regime had again been introduced in Sevastopol, that the measure was needed to eliminate an overload of electrical networks outside the region in order to prevent an accident in the entire energy system, and that a "2 through 6" schedule was being followed. Krymenergo, as reported by Vesti Krym at 8:26 a.m. Saturday, Nov 28, said that on the command of the federal System Operator, restrictions on the electric-power consumption regime had been introduced in the Republic of Crimea and that electricity supply to consumers had been limited.
outages.affected: Krymenergo, as reported by MK Krym at 9:33 a.m. Saturday, Nov 28 (12:33 a.m. CT Saturday, if Moscow time), said temporary restrictions on the consumption of electric power had been introduced in the Republic of Crimea on the direct command of the federal System Operator, and that specialists estimated the approximate duration of such outages would range from 3 to 9 hours. The same report said Krymenergo had previously introduced similar temporary consumption restrictions on the System Operator's order, including on Nov 23 and Nov 26, 2026, when outage schedules lasting from 3 to 6 hours were in effect for the same reason, and that electricity supply in Sevastopol had also been reduced to prevent accidents, with social facilities supplied in full. Krymenergo, as reported earlier Saturday by Vesti Krym at 8:26 a.m. Saturday, Nov 28 (11:26 p.m. CT Friday, Nov 27, if Moscow time), had said that on the federal System Operator's command, restrictions on the consumption of electric power had been introduced in the Republic of Crimea and that the supply of electricity to consumers had been limited, with an approximate outage duration of 3 to 9 hours. Sevastopolenergo, as reported by Lenta novostei Sevastopolya at 6:36 a.m. Saturday, Nov 28 (9:36 p.m. CT Friday, Nov 27, if Moscow time), said that on the command of the Black Sea Regional Dispatch Administration (ChRDU) dispatcher, a temporary electricity-supply restriction regime had been introduced in Sevastopol, a forced measure needed to relieve an overload of electric networks outside the region and prevent an accident in the entire power system. The same account said the city was following a "2 through 6" schedule: until 8:00 a.m., electricity would be supplied to the 2nd queue, with the others partially disconnected; until 10:00 a.m., electricity would be supplied to the 3rd queue, with the others partially disconnected; and that if the situation did not change, the queues would then be rotated on the same principle, with the schedule described as an approximate guide. MK Krym, in a report published at 9:23 a.m. Saturday, Nov 28 (12:23 a.m. CT Saturday, if Moscow time), citing Sevastopolenergo, said the supply of electricity to Sevastopol had been reduced on the ChRDU dispatcher's order to relieve the overload and prevent a system-wide accident, that because of the limited volume of electricity arriving in the city it was currently impossible to supply it according to the previous schedules, and that uninterrupted supply to socially significant facilities, including hospitals and pumping stations, was guaranteed. Kommersant, in a report dated 8:13 p.m. Friday, Nov 27 (11:13 a.m. CT Friday, if Moscow time), citing Sevastopolenergo, had said that on Saturday, Nov 28, from 5:00 a.m. to 12:00 a.m., the supply of electric power to legal entities in Sevastopol would be restricted because of emergency repair work on power-system facilities outside the city. No official customer count for Crimea or Sevastopol was found as of 6:00 AM CT Saturday, Nov 28 (3:00 p.m. Saturday, Nov 28, if Moscow time).
outages.start: Occupation sources said peninsula-wide interruptions began Oct 24, 2026; the 10-day restriction regime described by occupation officials began Wednesday, Nov 25, 2026, with Rossiyskaya Gazeta saying the restrictions began to apply at 6:50 a.m. Wednesday. outages.cause: Generation-capacity deficit in the national electric system. CiberCuba, in a report dated Friday, Nov 27, describing the official UNE Friday bulletin, said unit 1 of CTE Santa Cruz and unit 2 of CTE Felton remained in breakdown, and that unit 3 of CTE Santa Cruz, unit 5 of CTE Nuevitas, unit 1 of CTE Felton, and unit 5 of CTE Renté remained in maintenance, a picture it said was practically identical to that of the rest of the week, and that thermal-generation limitations amounted to 494 MW. The same account said Thursday's solar photovoltaic parks produced 3,393 MWh, with a maximum of 528 MW, and that solar generation does not cover the deficit in the evening peak period, when demand is highest.
outages.affected: CiberCuba's main outage page, updated at 6:14 a.m. Saturday, Nov 28, Cuba time (5:14 a.m. CT), said it was still showing the official UNE bulletin of Friday, Nov 27, because a Saturday official part did not yet contain sufficient national figures, and that Saturday reports from the Empresa Eléctrica de La Habana were local and did not allow a national SEN balance to be established. According to that page and CiberCuba's official-parts archive, the Friday UNE bulletin forecast 1,630 MW of affectation during the peak-demand period. Availability of the SEN at 6:00 a.m. Cuba time Friday, Nov 27 (5:00 a.m. CT), was 1,075 MW, demand was 2,100 MW, and 1,035 MW were already without service at that hour. For the evening peak, UNE estimated availability of 1,100 MW against demand of 2,700 MW, a deficit of 1,600 MW, and a forecast affectation of 1,630 MW. The same Friday official report estimated a midday Friday affectation of 1,300 MW, and recorded the previous day's (Thursday, Nov 26) peak affectation as 1,689 MW at 6:40 p.m. Cuba time (5:40 p.m. CT). CiberCuba's Nov 28 daily outage summary, citing the Empresa Eléctrica de La Habana, reported Saturday local circuit affectations and restorations in Havana from a generation-capacity deficit, including a 131 MW affectation in Havana at 12:05 a.m. Saturday, Nov 28, Cuba time (11:05 p.m. CT Friday, Nov 27), and later Saturday morning affectations on named circuits, including SR830 (Reparto Delicias) and P314 from 5:21 a.m. Saturday, Cuba time (4:21 a.m. CT), as well as restorations in circuits serving areas of Arroyo Naranjo, Marianao, and Boyeros. No official UNE Saturday national bulletin and no official national customer count was found as of 6:00 AM CT Saturday, Nov 28 (7:00 a.m. Saturday, Nov 28, Cuba time).

outages.cause: A collapse of a 275kV transmission tower in Ranau early Thursday morning, Nov 26, 2026, which Sabah Electricity said affected the west-to-east-coast transmission grid. The collapse of tower T313, detected at 6:04 a.m. Thursday, severed two transmission circuits linking Sabah's west and east coasts, according to Sabah Electricity, as reported by The Star, Malay Mail, H Metro, and Sinar Daily. Sabah Electricity's chief executive officer, Datuk Mohd Yaakob Jaafar, as reported by The Star at 8:48 p.m. Thursday, Nov 26, Malaysia time, said the tower's foundation along the banks of the Liwagu River was washed away following persistent heavy rains, resulting in the collapse of the tower, which is part of the grid that transmits 295 megawatts of electricity to the east coast. After the collapse, east-coast supply has been coming from existing generation in Sandakan and Tawau, supported by mobile generators and a battery energy storage system, with rotational load shedding because that local capacity is not enough to meet demand, according to Sabah Electricity accounts reported Friday by H Metro, The Star, and Sinar Daily.
outages.affected: Sabah Electricity, as reported by The Star at 6:01 p.m. Saturday, Nov 28, Malaysia time (4:01 a.m. CT Saturday), said in a progress update on its Facebook page that its technical team had completed installation of the main temporary Emergency Restoration System (ERS) tower structure at 1:45 p.m. Saturday, Nov 28, Malaysia time (11:45 p.m. CT Friday, Nov 27), and would next install the tower's crossarms and supporting components in preparation for installing transmission cables. The same report said the collapse had affected 153,599 registered consumers and that full supply restoration was targeted by Dec 3 at the latest. Daily Express, in a Saturday, Nov 28, report citing Bernama and Sabah Electricity Chief Operating Officer Mohd Riza Zalmee Mohd Ghazali speaking at the site in Kampung Sagindai Lama, said electricity supply in several districts along Sabah's east coast had been restored to 60 percent as of 1:00 p.m. Saturday, Nov 28, Malaysia time (11:00 p.m. CT Friday, Nov 27). The same account said the Thursday 6:04 a.m. collapse of tower T313 had severed two transmission-line circuits, disrupting supply in eight districts and affecting 153,599 registered consumers; that the east-coast transmission network was restored by 6:00 p.m. on the day of the incident and generation units in the region resumed full operation by 8:00 p.m. that evening; but that rotational power rationing continued because of a shortfall in available generation capacity, since nearly half of east-coast supply had been drawn from the west coast. The same report quoted Mohd Riza Zalmee as saying the company was striving to complete restoration ahead of the initial timeline, and that based on preliminary assessments and current progress, and provided the weather remained favorable, it was aiming to complete recovery earlier, by Dec 1; the report said Sabah Electricity had initially targeted full restoration by Dec 2. Prime Minister Datuk Seri Anwar Ibrahim, as reported by Malay Mail, first published at 4:10 p.m. Saturday, Nov 28, Malaysia time (2:10 a.m. CT Saturday), called on Sabah Electricity to restore supply earlier than scheduled and to give priority to temporary electricity for schools, examination centres, and critical public facilities, and said the disruption had hit up to eight districts after the Ranau tower collapse, affecting 153,599 consumers. Sabah Chief Minister Datuk Seri Hajiji Noor, as reported by Malay Mail, first published at 7:12 p.m. Saturday, Nov 28, Malaysia time (5:12 a.m. CT Saturday), citing Bernama, said he had been briefed by Sabah Electricity, that the tower repairs were expected to be completed within six days, that reserve power sources were being used, and that the situation had improved, although some areas might still experience minor supply shortages. Earlier Friday restoration-percentage figures, as reported by The Star and Bernama, had said that as of 3:00 p.m. Friday, Nov 27, Malaysia time (1:00 a.m. CT Friday), restoration in several east-coast districts had reached between 23 and 57 percent, with rotational load shedding still required.

outages.etr: Sabah Electricity, as reported by The Star at 6:01 p.m. Saturday, Nov 28, Malaysia time, said full supply restoration was targeted by Dec 3 at the latest. Daily Express, citing Bernama and Sabah Electricity Chief Operating Officer Mohd Riza Zalmee Mohd Ghazali on Saturday, said the company had initially targeted full restoration by Dec 2 and was now aiming to complete recovery earlier, by Dec 1, provided the weather remained favorable. Sabah Chief Minister Datuk Seri Hajiji Noor, as reported by Malay Mail at 7:12 p.m. Saturday, Malaysia time, citing Bernama, said the tower repairs were expected to be completed within six days. Prime Minister Datuk Seri Anwar Ibrahim, as reported by Malay Mail at 4:10 p.m. Saturday, Malaysia time, called on Sabah Electricity to restore supply earlier than scheduled. Earlier, Sabah Electricity chairman Datuk Saadiah Aziz, at a Thursday night press conference, had said the company was targeting Dec 2 for full grid restoration, and Chief Executive Officer Datuk Mohd Yaakob Jaafar, as reported by The Star on Thursday evening, had said they expect to restore normal power supply latest by Dec 3, aiming to restore the first transmission line on Dec 1 and both lines on Dec 2. Until then, rotational three-hour power-supply cycles, as previously announced by Sabah Electricity, remain in use because local east-coast generation cannot meet demand.

outages.cause: Planned electricity restrictions that Tavanir said began Sunday, Nov 22, 2026, because fuel shortages were disrupting power generation
outages.affected: The Washington Post, in a report dated Nov 26, 2026, and marked 5:00 a.m. EST (4:00 a.m. CT), said Iran is rationing electricity and scaling back government subsidies on bread and gasoline. Al Jazeera, in a Nov 25, 2026 feature, said Iran was rationing electricity and described scheduled power cuts that officials had announced this week because fuel shortages were disrupting generation. Nour News, in a report published at 3:35 p.m. Tuesday, 3 Azar 1405 (6:05 a.m. CT Tuesday, Nov 24, if Iran time), on Wednesday, Nov 25 (4 Azar 1405) outages in Tehran, said a review of available notices found no confirmed public timetable that specified outage hours for all Tehran neighborhoods, and that customers should check the status of their subscription in the Bargh Man system, because timing could differ by area and subscription. The National, in an article dated November 23, 2026, and marked updated at 5:00 a.m., said scheduled cuts had begun and quoted Tavanir CEO Mohammad Allahdad as saying the restrictions may take the form of a two-hour outage over two days, or a maximum of two hours each day if temperatures fall, and quoted President Masoud Pezeshkian, via Isna, on expected winter difficulties. Euronews Persian, in a report dated 7:42 a.m. GMT+1 Monday, Nov 23 (12:42 a.m. CT Monday), said planned electricity outages began on Sunday, Nov 22 (1 Azar 1405), that Tavanir had announced the cuts on Saturday because of fuel-supply limitations at power plants, and that electricity-industry officials in Khorasan Razavi, Qazvin, and Kermanshah had confirmed the start of the restrictions. The same Euronews report, citing Mashhad distribution-company spokesman Majid Hassan-Nejad, said each outage turn in Mashhad would last two hours, though it was not yet clear whether the restrictions would be applied daily or with a gap of several days; citing Qazvin distribution-company official Seyed Mohammad Ghaflabashi, that household and commercial customers there were subject to the restrictions; and, citing Mehr news agency and Kermanshah distribution-company CEO Seyed Hamed Hosseini, that two-hour outages in Kermanshah were being applied between 9:00 a.m. and 6:00 p.m. Iran International, in a report dated 1:17 p.m. GMT Sunday, Nov 22 (7:17 a.m. CT), said scheduled cuts were resuming and that Sunday reports from Tehran, Isfahan, Shiraz, Mashhad, Yazd, Kermanshah, and Ardabil described hours-long outages, often without notice, and quoted Allahdad on restrictions beginning Nov 22 because of fuel shortages. Nour News, in a report dated 8:09 a.m. Iran time Sunday, Nov 22, or 1 Azar 1405 (10:39 p.m. CT Saturday), and Eghtesad Online, in a report dated 8:29 a.m. Iran time Sunday (10:59 p.m. CT Saturday) that cited Nour News, said planned electricity restrictions began that day and, citing the Tavanir chief executive, that the new restrictions may take the form of a two-hour outage over two days, or a maximum of two hours each day, that the timing is not fixed and may change with network conditions, and that customers would be informed through the Bargh-e Man system and app, the Bale messenger app, and text messages. Tavanir had announced on Saturday, Nov 21, that planned electricity restrictions on households and businesses would begin on Sunday, Nov 22, because fuel shortages were disrupting power generation, according to Iran International in a report dated 5:11 p.m. GMT Saturday, Nov 21 (11:11 a.m. CT), and to RFE/RL. Anar News, in a report updated at 12:05 a.m. UTC Sunday, Nov 22 (6:05 p.m. CT Saturday), citing BBC Persian, also said planned power outages began in Iran on Sunday, Nov 22, because of fuel shortages at power plants. A review of available Thursday, Nov 26 (5 Azar 1405), public notices found no confirmed official Tavanir nationwide timetable that listed Thursday outage hours for all regions or for all Tehran neighborhoods; earlier Nour News reporting had similarly said customers should check the Bargh Man system because timing could differ by area and subscription. No official nationwide customer count was found as of 12:00 PM CT Thursday, Nov 26 (9:30 p.m. Thursday, Nov 26, Iran time). Rechecked 6:00 AM CT Saturday, Nov 28 (3:30 p.m. Saturday, Nov 28, Iran time), no official nationwide Tavanir timetable of Saturday outage hours for all regions, no official nationwide customer count, and no official announcement that the planned restrictions had ended, was found.

outages.cause: Drone attacks on power stations and other electricity infrastructure during the war between the Rapid Support Forces and the Sudanese Armed Forces
outages.affected: No official customer count. Al Jazeera, in a report dated Nov 27, 2026, last updated at 2:10 p.m. Makkah time (5:10 a.m. CT Friday), described continuing electricity interruptions in Omdurman, west of Khartoum, that were delaying work at leather workshops and other small businesses, and said that over two weeks 15 electricity transformer stations in Gedaref, Khartoum, Gezira, Red Sea, Sennar, White Nile, South Kordofan, Blue Nile, River Nile, and Northern states had been attacked and heavily damaged, causing power cuts in a number of cities. The same report referred to accounts from earlier in November that the Rapid Support Forces had continued to bomb Sudanese electricity and fuel stations with drones. Drop Site News, in a Nov 20, 2026 report from Khartoum, said a particularly intense wave of drone strikes at the end of October and into November targeting power stations, fuel supplies, and electricity infrastructure had brought the country's power grid to the brink of collapse, and that two weeks after the wave of attacks, major substations remained out of service. Shaker Ismail, an engineer with the Sudanese Electricity Company, told Drop Site that repairing some of the country's most important power facilities could take months or longer, that high-capacity transformers and digital control systems had been damaged, and that replacement transformers must be manufactured to order abroad. Ismail said the Um Dabakir thermal power plant in White Nile State was badly damaged in an Oct 29 strike and forced to shut down, and that the Al-Markhiyat substation west of Omdurman was put out of service after an Oct 27 strike. Rechecked 6:00 AM CT Saturday, Nov 28 (1:00 p.m. Saturday, Nov 28, Sudan time), no later official national customer count or official restoration timetable, and no official Saturday, Nov 28, update, was found.
